rv.q: This was another version which had theatrical flair amongst some theatrical flaws.

Williams’ play, directed by Ewan Downie, does a decent job of recounting the events of the day, taking the real words of real people from interviews and accounts, and distributing them between three energetic performers – Umar Butt, Adam Tompa and Leticia Sanchez – but it could do a lot more.
Leaving the Citz, one carries the lingering echo of a community's defiant chant – a timely reminder that when the vans arrive on our streets, our greatest defence is each other.
As with many works of formally ambitious theatre, however, where there are some genuinely successful moments, there are also some which miss their target.
Williams’ play channels the mixed emotions of those who were caught up in events as the world watched.

Whilst there is much promise, excitement and intentional storytelling to appreciate in this staging of inspiring modern local history through dance-theatre, it fails to reach the heartening heights of the deft, exemplary recreation it aspires to achieve and, at points, demonstrates it can deliver.

cn.t: Critics praise "These Are Our Neighbours" for its poignant theatrical reflection on the 2021 Kenmure Street protest, with reviewers commending its community-focused storytelling and timely exploration of Glasgow's collective resistance to immigration enforcement.
